reviews.text: I like Terra Randoma. I have an In-Progress Let's Play here if interested: https://youtu.be/0IkXQWdmTGs And I will of course be updating this review as I progress further in the game. That being said, let me say this: Terra Randoma is Fun. At the start, the game Feels like Morrowind, with the 5 mains skills or your character, picking the Star sign, and starting on a ship. Terra Randoma does 1 better though, letting you make landfall where you want, not just directly to a sleepy swamp town. Playing the game I got a real Mount & Blade Feel, with the services you can get in the towns, like purchasing weapons, armor, and supplies, and speaking to the lord in their keep, or talking to someone at the inn for a quest. Escort quests, item retrieval quests, kill quests, all are here. Of course, this is a 2D Fantasy RogueLike, not a 3D Mass Combat Simulation, so there are differences, but Terra Randoma has Dungeons and Lairs you can Quest in, and Magic! You don't often see full Procedural World Generation in a Rogue Like, or in most games really; if present in a RogueLike, it's usually just the dungeons. Not in Terra Randoma! The Entire World is Procedurally Generated, at the start! And it's not just that the world mass is randomized at the start; the World both Reacts to You, and Changes around You. New Quests are offered, the towns might have safe roads, decreasing the cost of goods, while Famines, Plagues, and Riots might break out in the cities, reducing the benefits they can provide to you. The Prosperity of the Towns rises and falls, the prices of goods changing accordingly, making weapons, armor, and potions either more in reach, or more expensive due to demand. Though Terra Randoma is Early Access, it is rock stable, solid fun, and is being developed by a dedicated dev team determined to make it the best it be. Sound good to me! I look forward to playing more if it. Note: Terra Randoma is a Traditional Rogue Like, but the Perma Death is optional in this one, in case it's not to your taste. It's to my taste. Terra Randoma. With a Charming Table-Top aesthetic, and Detailed World Simulation, Terra Randoma is one Turn Based Tactics focused Traditional Rogue Like that is more than just a Dungeon Crawler, it is a World Crawler! Crawl this World with Me?

I was waiting for this game to be released and it didn't surprise. Well made roguelike RPG. Heavy focus on mechanics, without any unnecessary story for you to skip. Balanced, neat, easy to understand. I'm expecting the UI to be improved a bit and more content during Early Access. Keep up the good work guys!

Fun procedural turn-based sandbox: You're no one when you finaly reach Terra Randoma. You'll have to survive the wild, be recognized as a worthy hero or die trying ^^ The procedural events related to settlements give life to the world (impacting the economy mainly through events like plague, road block, seasonal festivities...) and break the routine of going to settlement "A" to buy "x" then go to settlement "B" to sell "x" and buy "y". Events "on the road" also bring sparks of life to the world (more are coming in the following weeks and months). Combat and dungeon crawling are tough early on and keeping an "ace in your sleeve" is a good idea. This early version is stable and performs well, no major issue to report. Keep in mind that the game will remain in early access for about a year so while you can already complete a run, content will grow in the following weeks/months.

Its got some major potential for sure. The biggest problem right now is that there doesn't seem to be much in the way of goals. You're mostly doing procedural quests that get gradually harder, getting gradually better loot, and leveling up as you do so. It wasn't clear what my long term goal was. If I could give the developer advice, it would be to give the players a bit more agency in terms of self established goals. It felt very much like the only strategic agency I had was in placing my skill points. It'd be nice if there were larger strategic goals I could pursue to differentiate my characters/strategy. I imagine as content as added, the game will continue to be good, and continue to grow. As it stands, it was a fun romp for 10 hours or so, and I will definitely come back. Worth the price, worth keeping an eye on.

I like roguelikes, ironman games, procedural generation, and turn based combat. All the things that this game offered me. But, this is one of the most bare-bones games I have seen in awhile. What you see in the first thirty minutes is about all that you can expect from this. It's... fine. But it isn't 15-dollars fine. It might be worth five bucks, but not more.

updated Nov 15 2023 +"your chance to hit this is 57%"; miss it eight times in a row. This happens all the time. Seriously. It's statistically improbable I'm that unlucky, something is just broken about resolving hits. +Avg cost of fight traveling overworld far outstrips what you get/sell typically. This issue has gotten better since April 2023. +HP doesn't regenerate naturally. +Everything is overly reliant on potions which are vastly overpriced considering how little everything sells for at base (items are 2x to 5x markup to buy, anything you sell for 1/3 or less). +Baseline stamina regen is like 1 or less per turn. It rapidly degrades into the toilet as you pickup loot. A basic move that you'd start with costs ~20 stamina and it doesn't get much better. +Alchemy and cooking sounds great, as if you could make your own potions that are required for doing anything, but because it's absolutely RNG I'm practically never getting what I need to make the particular potions I want because there's no way to find the particular ingredients I need. In reality, although you *could* make the potions you need, it's absolute blind luck if you get the ingredients you need. I hate it.

[h1]IN A WORD: [b]WORTHWHILE[/b] [/h1] [h1]IN A NUTSHELL:[/h1] [quote=] [b]WHAT TO EXPECT:[/b] Traditional Roguelike. Fantasy setting & theme. Focused character generation. 7x classes, 12 starsigns, 3x stats, 15x skills. Procedurally generated world with settlement statuses. IGOUGO turn-based combat. Melee and ranged combat. Tactical combat abilities via talent stones. Renewable quests. Non-persistent dungeons and encounter locations. 100+ enemies with tactical abilities and variants. Large item inventory. Limited carry capacity, no permanent storage nor stackable items. Hardcore challenge. Singleplayer only. [b]ACHIEVEMENTS:[/b] NONE. [b]STATUS:[/b] IN EARLY ACCESS. ACTIVE DEV. [b]WHEN TO BUY:[/b] BUYERS PEROGATIVE.[/quote] [i]More info below....[/i] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2409412305 [h1]THE LOWDOWN:[/h1] Terra Randoma (TR) is a fantasy-themed roguelike where the protagonist sets forth on an adventure to discover the threat posed to a procedurally generated world. Unlike an RPG there is no scripted plot, rather a story and optional main quest emerges. Character generation assigns one of seven classes and one of twelve star-signs affecting STR, DEX and INT stats and fifteen skills. On their travels players must fight, gain experience, gold and fame, and manage their character's health, stamina and hunger without the aid of any allies. Beyond its Unity-made production values a 'different' world populated by eight settlements awaits the hero(ine). These consist of traders (armour, weapons, accessories, food and potions) and a tavern to regain health and overcome hunger. Hubs provide specific adventuring services. Towns possess two quest-givers. Fluctuating statuses make the world come alive influencing factors such as prosperity or safety near these settlements. Completed quests affect a character's reputation with the townsfolk. Exploration occurs overland with the character moved one tile. Dangerous, neutral or friendly encounters occur while traversing the wilderness, even at sea. Camping, hunting or foraging is permitted to recuperate health and hunger between locations. Choices that are skill-related or otherwise, to interact, flee or fight are given in menu form. Encounters occur on a reduced tile-based map which also disappear once exited. A simple one action IGOUGO turn-based combat system is implemented. Where the weapons held and equipment worn, potions and talent stones imbued with special powers augment the character's abilities. Players will get to fight over a hundred enemy types and variants. Some with their own tactical powers. A limited inventory allows for the collection of a hundred or more weapons, armour, food, potions and accessory types. Players can ignore the main quest and focus on repeating quests found within randomly generated dungeons. These locations are non-persistent and can only be left and returned to, if the objective is active or they disappear permanently, including any items that were left behind. There are five difficulties and the selection of permadeath is optional. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2362905192 [h1]THE GOOD:[/h1] + Well-crafted open world. + Mature encounter, item and enemy generating systems. + Good breadth of random encounters with a host of enemy or neutral NPCS. Traders, thieves, traps, request for help, kidnappers of escort quests, hunters, even combat on ships when at sea. + Complex combat engine with status effects such as: Stunned, confused, slowed, etc. + Variation of tactics in combat through the use of 21+ talent stones. Inc. transforming into a grizzly bear. + Impressive array of detailed inventory items. + Lots of different enemies, with variants such as extra loot, strength, armoured or speed. Plus many with their own tactical abilities. + Good balanced enemy AI. Will attack or retreat depending on situation. + Permadeath is optional. + Active EA dev. Taking suggestions and fixing bugs. [h1]THE BAD:[/h1] - Needs permanent item storage, larger inventory and stackable items. - Items from killed enemies never drop more than once on same tile. - Simple one slot save system. Lets hope the save never corrupts. - Some overlapping GUI sub-screens. - Needless loss of reputation when leaving areas just to sell items before returning. - No buy back facility at stores. - No item comparison facility in inventory. - Can only collect from containers. Cannot switch out from a full inventory. - Stock assets sounds. - Dungeons need more activities. Traps. Secret areas. - No allies make for a lonely experience. - BUG: Items held out of inventory when returning back to map screen are lost. [h1]AND THE REST:[/h1] * Procedurally generated world offers some replayability. * Basic fixed overland grid-based map. * Five difficulties. * Good-sized amount of RP attributes and skills. (3x stats, 7x classes, 12x Starsigns) * Simple pretty polygon-formed graphics. * Intimate encounters on small maps with only a handful of enemies. * Character level cap planned at 39. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2361442408 [h1]ANALYSIS:[/h1] TR may currently be in Early Access but there is already a substantial amount of content to draw in fans of traditional style rogue-likes. The systems and processes to generate quests, encounters, dungeons, items and enemies are already brimming with enough variations as to keep interest up when playing. Differences between plays seems to lie with the play style chosen; classes and the skills focused on. The generation of quests, settlement locations, loot and random encounters does eventually become familiar, feeling samey. Visuals reminded me of playing tabletop RPGs with Lego people. They are bright and colourful. Makes a change from the pixelated or 2D styles seen before. Attention to detail is great with strong identifiable enemies models and fully updating character avatar. A strong GUI design, the inclusion of hints and the use of menu driven options combined to make TD very accessible to novice gamers. The initial challenge of learning how the game plays is benign enough to ease players into a good rhythm. Encounters became harder with boss fights beginning to feel hardcore at around Level 11. Something to be expected. Combat was a simple affair. Talent stones providing tactical elements to fights. Basic enemies were swatted aside. Bosses felt tanky without correctly allocated stats and stronger weapons. Becoming surrounded was fatal vs enemies that paralyse. With their friends that inflict damage over time and it was 'adios muchachos.' Loot drops were fine, if a little lack-lustre in terms of useful items. Most were there to sell for funds to buy tablet stones, potions and skill points. There are a couple of places where the game falls short. My biggest gripe is the limited inventory. No permanent storage or stackable items. Resulting in items being left to dissolve permanently once an area is left. Overall there is very little wrong with TR. It could do with some balance passes and additional content. More monsters, items and locations. As of this review the dev continues to post updates with fixes and some content. TR reminds me a lot of SotS: The Pit and that game was not built in a day! [h1]VERDICT:[/h1] Given my experience with TR it is fun to play and easy to pickup. Combat has some depth but is uncomplicated making for some addictive gameplay. If the dev continues to update TR this game will become even better. If they choose to address the issues highlighted this could command the time of anyone who enjoys this type of game. Even though it is in Early Access I would recommend this to anyone who is interested. For me, thats a first! Do you like Tabletop Games? But, you don´t like preparing them before playing? Then you are on the right Place here. Welcome to TERRA RANDOMA. This one Man Project presents a very big World to be explored. Choose one of seven Classes, choose a Star Sign (They will give you a Bonus), name your Hero, choose your Difficulty and then get ready for the World. Oh, i forgot. You can also decide if you like to have perma death or not. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2368124463 You will always start on a Boat and reach an Island. Every time you start new, the Island is randomly generated, so every Adventure is a new one. After leaving your Boat a whole Island is waiting for you. Before you run into your Adventure, one important thing. Have always an Eye of your Status Bars. There is a Food Bar, so don`t get starve. If you run out of Food, make a Camp and go hunting or search for Food. Your Camp will show you in percent how succesfull you can be in these two options. All right, then lets go. While you wander around the Island you will stumble in little Events. It can be an attack, or an old ruin, maybe something to hunt or just a Person who needs help. There is very much to explore and you will also reach Citys. Here you can rest, eat and get Quests. There are also higher Quests, but you first have to rise your reputation by doing other Quests to get the high ones. Quests can be everything. An Escort, a Dungeon, a Ruin and much more. Search every Place for Loot. Get from NO ONE to THE ONE. From hero to zero. It is all up too you. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2368124240 That brings us back to my Opening Speech with the Tabletop. The Graphic is wonderfull Old School Tabletop Style. You move a typical Tabletopfigure over the Map and that goes also for the Encounters. Simple but addicting. That goes also for the Fights. If you have enough experience, you can also level up your upcoming Hero and raise your Stats to become stronger. Armor, Weapons and other Equipment can be easily overseen and moved from one Place to the Other. That goes also for buying and selling. The Title Theme is very nice and the Sound Effects fit in very well. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2368125120 So, if you are looking for an addicting but simple RPG without learning a whole Handbook in a Tabletop World, then this is for you. A very big Thanks to the Dev for this wonderfull Game. Good Job. Thank YOU for Reading. This is an open-world rogue-like with optional permadeath, and procedural generation of dungeons and items. You can choose certain starting classes, but your class does not in any way limit you from focusing on different abilities as you progress through the game. It merely determines what advantages you start the game with. And all abilities/spells are purchasable by all characters, if you have the money to do so. I do want to address some complaints that I've seen: Regarding Stun-Locks (and Freeze Locks, for that matter) -- when I first started playing, they were a problem for me. Since I figured out how to deal and avoid and defend against that, I have not died once from that happening (I've still died from stupid carelessness, as is common in a roguelike, but never from a stun or freeze lock). With regards to the potential to have gear destroyed -- first, that's been potentially true in many traditional roguelikes, so that's not new. But second, again, once I realized the multiple ways to avoid that happening, I've never again lost any gear. As you learn the game better, it should NEVER be an issue. With regards to repetitiveness, yeah, there is a bit of that, as there is with most traditional roguelikes. But there's also been a lot of new content since I started playing, so be patient. Certain types of enemies and maps require slightly different tactics, adding some variety to the game. And the upcoming new content that has been previewed should add quite a bit.

Hard to rate this, the game was fun but very frustrating, every character I had has died the same way. Backpack full of potions, food and buffs on, stun-locked for 10-12 turns in a row...dead. almost always from a random encounter I have a 5% chance to evade, even with points in wilderness survival. Kinda over it, as no way out of stun-lock just means every character is a bad rng from dying. If I had made a bad choice or pushed my luck and died I would be okay with it, but full 150+ life to dead while stun locked is pretty much a fun killer.
FUN, BASIC GAME, I PLAY ON EASY DIFFICULTY. ITS ENTERTAINING.

[h3]Adventure awaits[/h3] If you're having a hard time finding other people to play a quick round of tabletop then Terra Randoma might be your quick and satisfying solution. While it is labeled as traditional roguelike, there are still three different difficulty settings to choose from of which only the Ironman-mode is "real" permadeath. Loads of different classes don't actually mean that your pushed into one style of play. They are rather a gentle way to provide a basic ground for your novice beginner skills, yet still unfamilar with how things work in this new world of yours. Be anything and learn everything, provided you assign the correct stats. To do so, you, of course, have to level up. Here is where things become a bit difficult. [h3]Saving saves[/h3] Let me tell you the story of Oleander the Tempest, a ruthless yet skilled master of the arts of combat and magic alike. He heard of a legend. A legend that spoke about an ancient evil, sleeping in deep caverns, dreaming of the destruction it unleashes onto the world only to sink into a slumber again afterwards. To find these caverns, one must collect five pieces of a tablet, each clutched in the hand of a lord. Every one of them expects Oleander to earn their respect and solve dangerous quests, master difficult dungeons and in return earn one piece of the most important tablet. So Oleander set out to become the greatest hero of all times. On day 9 he got stung by a bee. On day 10 he died. The end. So, what is written above actually happened in my first attempt to play through Terra Randoma. I simply forgot to save and when I died, everything was lost. Had I chosen the Hero mode, I would have respawned in the nearest town, having lost some gold and xp but, alas, I chose Wayfarer mode, where you can save everytime and everywhere - but you have to do it! The lore I recited is the actual ingame story and gives your otherwise completely randomized world some sort of needed structure, although I don't praise its originality. The ability to randomize your world and every quest in it comes with the price of being just vague enough to make sense. [h3]The passionate Widow[/h3] If you made it alive into the first town, you'll be greeted with the most usual stuff. A store, a tavern and the town's lord. In the tavern you'll meet somebody who almost always gives you some sort of quest. Quests not only reward xp and gold but also some very precious reputation. The latter is needed if you want to get the chance to get a difficult mission from the town's lord and to ultimately get one of his tablet shards. Repeat this until you can find and beat the final boss. I find this part of the game, namely the writing and story-telling, to be the weakest. I'm an avid lover of roguelikes hence I know that, while not forgetting some outstanding exceptions, story is most often not what makes you play again and again. Since Terra Randoma is labeled as RPG as well, I still have to look at the Roleplaying part. Quests suffer the Daggerfall syndrom in a way that they are always randomized, putting different places and people together. Go there, kill this, go there, save this person. You don't actually have a personality as none of the NPCs have unless you'd call an adjective a fleshed out character. So, while all of this sounds bad, or at least not very convincing to play Terra Randoma, I still stuck with it. Why? Because the gameplay is where this piece of random tabletop dungeon simulator really shines. [h3]Heros are made, not born[/h3] As said earlier, starting classes only give you a pair of two feet to stand on so you can walk into your first battles. If you want to run, you might have to think about it for a second. Which stat do I want to bolster and what is the best complementary equipment? Increasing strength increase your HP but Stamina as well. It is needed to perform a multitude of actions and, if you're running out of it, chances are you're standing still in a fight without a chance to hit back. It also increases your Food, because, yes, you also have a hunger meter that depletes with many actions. But what about Dexterity? Increasing Defence and therefor increasing the chance to avoid hits sounds good, right? By now you know what I'm talking about. There are loads of skills, like Two-Handed Weapons, Intimidation, Ranged Combat and Alchemy to just name some of them. Each of these further build and create your very own and unique playstyle. Every 5 points in them reward you with a special bonus like gaining speed whilst only using heavy armor or a 50% chance that your lockpick won't break on chests. All of these are pretty common rpg stuff but it is enough to keep the actual gameplay interesting. Throughout your journeys, you'll not only have random encounters with multiple and different enemies but also find curious and special events. I have to admit though that they usually all lead to some sort of combat engagment - which is great! Combat is pure and simple fun. While you move, the enemy moves as well. All attacks happen simultaneously as do spells. You can still peek into your backpack and drink a potion, of which there are quite many. Not only can you cure poison or reagain health but also transform into a bat or a bear, make yourself invisible or immune to certain negative events and debuffs. Terra Randoma shines most when you forget how basic the storytelling is whilst leveling up your character. The game feels punishing sometimes but not unfair. I learned from early mistakes I made like I rather bought additional potions before I went on my journey instead of hoarding all the coin. There is no use for it when you get killed by a giant bee anyway. Also, towns will very often have positive or negative events which will influence your visit. Sometimes food will be overflowing and you can stock up very cheap. Coming back later you might be greeted by an epidemic, making shops paying very much for potions - but not selling any in return. These random events make your journey a bit more interesting but challenging as well. I actually died outside of a town once because I wasn't able to pay a potion in their shop. If you find the overworld harsh, wait until you make your way into the dungeons. Enemies in bigger numbers roam the caverns whilst traps make it even more easy for you to die. In return you find more chests, bigger and better equipment and other useful loot. These are real challenges that, once overcome, really show how good or bad your character build functions and were by far the most fun part for me in the game. [h3]Last words[/h3] So, Terra Randoma is a very enjoyable game that focuses on character building, combat and the players ability to learn and adapt. Personally I might enjoy it even more if there was a pure dungeon mode, without any need of finishing many of these rather mundane quests. As much as I enjoy to help a widow in need, I find it hard to find value in said quest if the combat is the only thing that mattered in the first place anyways. Maybe implementing a dungeon mode is too much to ask for so, for now, I stick to make my way into combat as fast as possible. The replayabilty is very high due to a randomized world and different classes with no set skill tree. Grinding is not necessary but I found it to be actually quite enjoyable because the combat offered enough depth to make every battle just a little bit different. The overall look and feel of the game is very reminiscent of a tabletop and as such might offer a new home to players who otherwise don't enjoy roguelikes or rpgs. Get out, help those widows in need and slay that evil kraken in the smartest way possible! SUMMARY: A must-buy charming Roguelike Open World game that delivers all the classics - monsters, quests, and more, in a procedural open world. It scratches that itch for fulfilling quests and wandering about with some surprises as you task your way to fighting the Big Bad. Streamlined yet deep, if you want a game of quest-taking, equipment-maxing, and monster-mashing that's replayable, this is a must-buy. Terra Randoma feels like it fell out of an alternate 90's. You could imagine some parallel universe where we all played it, where there was a port or remake, and where people still discuss speedrunning it to this day. It's a game that takes the essence of many Roguelikes and other games - Elder Scrolls, etc.- and combines them. The game is your basic fantasy adventure - wander the world, explore, take quests, smash monsters, build characters. It does this in a high-detail, low complication way that lets you have all sorts of adventure without filler - grab quests, go to dungeons, smash monsters, buy stuff, etc. It also does this with a charming "Tabletop RPG feel" - even the maps appear to be on a tabletop! The core plot?: There's a great evil and you decided to go smash it. Then the game kicks in . . . So what have we got? CHARACTER BUILDING: Start with a class, a starsign, and some swappable "skill stones." As you level up you can level skills and attributes, as well as buying more skill points and skill stones to use. You get plenty of ways to customize your character, and different elements interact, giving you a lot to think about. "Skill Stones", which grant special abilities are swappable, allowing you to customize your character easily. EQUIPMENT: Of course there's equipment - mostly weapons, armor, and potions. A lot of them have different effects and benefits, so balance carefully and look for synergies. Fortunately there's no pesky identification. There is a lack of the classic scrolls and wands - potions do it all (a lava potion solves a lot of issues). TRAVEL: Each character gets their own unique Open World to wander in. There are cities, towers, dungeons, and terrain to contend with. Plenty of random events will give you things to do, monsters to avoid, ruins to explore, and treasure to find. The seasons change, altering what you encounter and how your spells work. Every trip from place to place is it's own adventure. TOWNS AND MORE: Towns give you a chance to rest, buy things, and take quests and missions. Some special towns provide unique services or purchase items at an increased rate. Towns may also have random visitors that can help you. Random town statuses can also change up your experience - save money during an alchemy festival, liberate a town from bandits, and more . . . QUESTS: Quests can be found in towns and wandering around and can involve rescuing people, fighting monsters, escorting people, digging up treasures and more. They don't just pay gold, they affect your reputation and the town economy. In turn, that may unlock better options and quests vital to the aforementioned evil-smashing. DUNGEONS: Of course there are dungeons. These have monsters, treasure, etc. They're randomly generated for the purpose of quests and vanish when done. They're also not overly big so you can dungeoneer in 20 minutes or less not 30 hours. You'll also want to be tactical in choices - there are traps, hazards, exploding barrels, treasure . . . COMBAT: Combat is a big part of the game. A lot of it is driven by a mix of stamina, skill stones, weapon choice, and of course pounding potions. Combat isn't too complicated, but there's enough interactive factors that thought pays off, while not thinking gets you killed. Positioning and moving plays a big role. CRAFT AND GO DEEP: Learn lore to unlock quests. Brew potions. Cook foods. Upgrade equipment It's all the classic adventuring with a few extra twists. BASE BUILDING: From cabin to castle, you can build up to three bases to make your life easier. Store equipment, fix armor, and more! Since the lands are randomized, a strategically placed base can make a difference. And beware of unwelcome visitors . . . INTERACTIONS: All of the above interact together. A character may level a skill that gets them cheaper prices, a chance for thievery may impact your reputation, and a new item helps you battle evil. The game really shines in all of its (mostly) straightforward elements playing together - and there's a few surprise interactions. Sure being the best cook sounds simple, but when your best foods give you huge buffs and healing . . . CLEVER MECHANICS: The game also boasts some clever mechanics. You accumulate "Lore" which lets you purchase various things. Skills require you to think about interactions and how to spend to get "the next big bonus" - like being able to poison the undead. You'll get some nice mechanic surprises here. A RESPONSIVE DEV: The Dev is open to feedback and listens to it and keeps upgrading the game. If you have a good idea, they will work it into the game! REPLAYABLE: Each randomized game is a different world, classes play differently, meaning each game is it's own experience. Is it a must-buy? Yes if open-world roguelikes are your jam. This is a streamlined-but-not-shallow pile of monster mashing, equipment-maxing, skill building, and careful tactical decisions. Because no quest or part is overlong, you can pace yourself or dive in. If that appeals to you, then go ahead. For me? I got it in Early Access and played FOUR HOURS in one day. For many, I expect this game will be one they play, win, and come back to over years.

Despite Terra Randoma’s simplistic appearance and easy to follow mechanics, it’s not a game you master in just a couple of hours; there is a more under the hood here then just bumping into enemies like your average roguelike game. There’s a stamina system that is crucial for regulating your hero’s efficiency when battling foes and then you really have know how to manage your inventory. Make sure you are stocked with potions and food before venturing out, something that can be easier said than done since everything is costly. You need to weight in how much gold you are willing to spend on survivability at the cost of not expanding your character’s efficiency with new abilities. I’m not particular fond of potion driven mechanics but here it works well since everything is generally expensive, forcing you to make critical decisions. Like traditional roguelikes, the word is procedurally generated for unlimited replay value, and you get to decide if permadeath is something you wish to cope with. On top of this, I had the opportunity to chat with the dev team to report some minor issues - sweetest couple you will ever meet. An amazing and underrated game. An RPG where everything - including the world and the quests - is procedurally generated is a great concept for fans of turn-based combat, as there will always be fresh challenges and each game will be different. And the devs have really exploited this with really diverse character customisation and map generation options at the start, and a wide range of skills to be learned, and loads of equipment and other loot to be found. Having played the game on the hardest difficulty levels I can confirm the game is very well balanced even for veterans of the genre looking for a challenge. And there is a helpful overall summary of your progress available, that makes sure you do not start feeling lost amid the randomness and gives an overall feeling of direction. [b]Terra Randoma[/b] is a turn-based dungeon crawler (and also a wilderness crawler) that can be played as a roguelike (with permanent death) or as an RPG (with no punishment or almost no punishment for dying), and it’s clearly a labor of love that deserves your attention if you’re into these genres. The first thing that stands out in this game is that the whole world is procedurally generated, not just the dungeons. When starting a game you can even choose the kind of map you want (think Sid Meier’s Civilization), which adds to the replayability. The permadeath setting (called Ironman in the game) is also separate from the game’s difficulty, which is a nice touch. During the character creation process, you can mix several classes with different starting perks, leading to dozens of combinations. As you might have noticed, the game’s graphics resemble tabletop games, and are very beautiful in my opinion. What’s not beautiful (yet, I hope) are the sound effects and soundtrack, which can be easily muted, thankfully. You can play using only the mouse (with optional keyboard commands) and the interface is very big (for better or worse), which makes Terra Randoma a great choice for playing on laptops. The gameplay feels very strategic and tactical, constantly demanding from the player their full attention while dealing with the character’s resources, life, stamina and hunger. There’s also cooking and crafting, which usually are things I dismiss on roguelikes and RPGs, but in Terra Randoma they’re super handy and will literally save your life, especially since buying potions (already crafted) is super expensive and there are buffs you get from cooked food that you can’t buy anywhere, even if you have a lot of spare money, so it’s handy to invest some points (and time) in cooking and crafting. I have beaten the game with permadeath and on Normal difficulty, and it was mostly a breeze (it took me about 16 hours, more or less). Now I’m playing on hard and permadeath, and suddenly Terra Randoma became a tough as hell roguelike, which is something I really appreciate. There are also difficulties that are easier than Normal, so I believe this is a game that can appeal to all kinds of players. Overall, I’m having a great time, the developer is super active and communicative, and the gameplay feels very polished and satisfying. Yes, Terra Randoma it’s still tagged as Early Access, but it already feels like a complete game that will only get better from now on. Totally recommended! [b]May the tides bring you triumph![/b]

This is an excellent RPG with a very enjoyable game loop: get quest, stock up on materials, enter dungeon, explore, try not to die, collect loot, return. It's bite-sized instead of hugely sprawling: you can see the entire map on one screen, there are five towns, the dungeons have a fixed maximum size, and you can only do five quests at a time. That makes it easy to work your way through the game, and keeps you playing for just one more quest, one more item upgrade, and so on. It took me about 30 hours for one victory on normal difficulty.

Some nice ideas, but ultimately gets crushed by tedium and a shocking lack of basic QoL. The Tedious: [list] [*]Quest objectives almost always spawn on the far side of the map, and require a return trip to the quest giver to complete. [*]Random encounters are numerous, and despite a supposed variety, seem to mostly be the same five or six scenarios. [*]Difficult terrain, inclement weather, and status effects all slow the real-time movement of your character between squares. It's a turn-based game, there's no reason for this. [*]The dungeons are all the same, and you have to explore every randomly generated room to spawn the boss. [*]Special abilities all use stamina, which regenerates incredibly slowly. But guess what, your basic attacks also use stamina! Health doesn't regen at all. So for every minor battle you end up chugging 2 or 3 potions, and then have to spend your non-questing time just searching vendors to restock. [*]Equipment has durability. But repair kits are so plentiful that there's no real risk of your gear breaking at inopportune times. So it's just another tedious thing to keep an eye on. [*]Crafting skills are borderline useless because one of the two materials for every recipe is inexplicably rare. [/list] The Unquality of Life [list] [*]Remember when I said you have chug potions like a frat boy on Friday night? You can't assign potions to the hotbar, so you're constantly opening your (likely overcrowded) inventory to keep yourself alive. [*]You can't rebind keys. Movement uses the numpad, but 'wait' uses the spacebar; num-5 isn't even an alternate. For chugging potions, you're going be opening your (B)ackpack instead of (I)nventory. [*]Mouse movement is one square at a time. [*]The graphics settings are just 1 through 5, without any explanation or apparent effect beyond making the screen darker. The edges of the playing field have an incredibly distracting blur effect that can't be turned off. [*]Ambient sound effects in town are also terribly annoying and can't be turned off. [*]The game allows you to open just about any screen from any other screen, but then gets confused as to which screen to close when you hit the escape key. (Pro Tip: It should always be the last screen opened.) [/list] The dev appears to be finished with working on the game with the latest 'codex' update, so I wouldn't expect any improvements. All of the "features" I listed have been in the game for years at this point, anyway.

Terra Randoma is a turn-based roguelike RPG that thrives on unpredictability, player agency, and systems-driven storytelling. Developed and published by Deniz K., the game presents itself modestly at first, with a simple visual style and an unassuming interface, but it quickly reveals a dense web of mechanics and interactions that reward patience and experimentation. Rather than guiding the player through a tightly scripted narrative, Terra Randoma focuses on creating a world where stories emerge naturally through exploration, combat decisions, and the consequences of chance. The foundation of the experience lies in its procedurally generated world. Each new game drops the player onto a freshly created island, complete with its own geography, settlements, dungeons, and points of interest. These worlds can vary significantly in layout and scale, encouraging multiple playthroughs and ensuring that familiarity never turns into predictability. Exploration feels purposeful, as traveling across the map can lead to unexpected discoveries, whether that’s a struggling town in need of help, a dangerous ruin hiding valuable loot, or a random encounter that spirals into a major turning point for your character. The sense that anything could happen at any moment is one of the game’s strongest hooks. Combat is built around classic grid-based, turn-based mechanics that emphasize positioning, stamina management, and tactical foresight. Every action carries weight, and careless decisions can quickly lead to defeat, especially when facing stronger enemies or unfavorable terrain. Instead of traditional classes, Terra Randoma offers a highly flexible character system built around skills and special abilities, allowing players to shape their character freely over time. This openness encourages creative builds, whether you prefer brute-force melee combat, stamina-efficient survivability, or a hybrid approach that adapts to whatever the world throws at you. Abilities play a crucial role in defining combat flow. Special powers, learned through unique systems rather than rigid class trees, can dramatically change how battles unfold. Managing stamina becomes just as important as dealing damage, as overextending yourself can leave your character vulnerable at the worst possible moment. This balance between power and restraint gives combat a thoughtful pace, rewarding careful planning over impulsive aggression. Encounters feel less like puzzles with fixed solutions and more like dynamic problems shaped by terrain, enemy behavior, and available resources. Outside of combat, Terra Randoma leans heavily into survival and world interaction systems. Hunger, weather, time of day, and environmental conditions all influence decision-making, adding texture to exploration. Camping, cooking, and crafting are not side activities but essential tools for long-term success, providing buffs and recovery options that can mean the difference between survival and failure. These mechanics integrate smoothly with the broader gameplay loop, reinforcing the idea that preparation and adaptability are just as important as raw combat skill. Quests and progression are intentionally loose and organic. Rather than following a linear storyline, players pick up tasks from taverns, settlements, or chance encounters, shaping their own path through the world. Some quests resolve quickly, while others branch or evolve based on outcomes, creating a sense of continuity and consequence. Towns can change over time, relationships form through repeated interaction, and reputations subtly influence how the world responds to your presence. This approach allows Terra Randoma to feel more like a living sandbox than a checklist-driven RPG. Visually, the game adopts a minimalist, almost tabletop-inspired aesthetic that prioritizes clarity over spectacle. While it lacks flashy animations or detailed character models, this simplicity helps keep the focus on mechanics and decision-making. The interface presents information efficiently, making it easy to track resources, abilities, and status effects without overwhelming the player. Audio design is understated, serving primarily to support immersion rather than dominate attention, which fits the game’s contemplative and methodical tone. Difficulty and randomness are central to the experience, and they won’t appeal to everyone. Luck can play a significant role in encounters, and unexpected setbacks—including sudden character death—are part of the design philosophy. However, the game offers options that allow players to adjust how punishing the experience is, making it accessible to those who prefer a more forgiving RPG while still satisfying players who enjoy high-stakes roguelike tension. In the end, Terra Randoma is a game that values systems over spectacle and emergent stories over scripted drama. It rewards players who enjoy thinking through consequences, adapting to uncertainty, and learning from failure. While its presentation is modest and its pacing deliberately measured, the depth beneath the surface is substantial. For fans of turn-based tactical RPGs and roguelikes who appreciate freedom, replayability, and worlds shaped as much by chance as by choice, Terra Randoma offers a rich and quietly compelling adventure that grows more engaging the longer you spend with it. Rating: 8/10
